items.title: Cascadu interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019
items.q: I hooked up with some of the top players in Trinidad, guys like Len Boogsle Sharpe and Raf Robertson Clive Zanda — all those guys come from the calypso jazz tradition. And I just plugged right in.

ctx.x: That makes me smile because I think all the dues you paid in your other professions, even if you liked it — you know some people go through life and they have a job they don’t like and they just can’t wait to be retired and do something they like. It sounds — I’m just guessing that you liked the other things you did but now that you’re doing this it makes it all that much more fruitful for you.

Absolutely. Absolutely. Well I started, you know as I mentioned, I am from Trinidad. And I grew up in a folk culture. I was first a dancer. I started dancing at age five and went through until I was about fifteen, sixteen years old, dancing. All my life I was close to the drum. I remember where we lived in Fyzabad, which is deep south Trinidad. A lot of roots, a lot of culture. There was a shango yard not too far away up on the hill, and I used to hear the drums coming across at night when I was you know, about…

constant struggle between the sciences and the arts. The sciences and the arts. When I went to university, and I went to university to study biogeography because I wanted to do forestry and ecology and stuff. At York University there was a Caribbean performing group on the campus. And I figured since nobody here knew me I would try and, you know, see if I could get back to a little bit of dance. And it so happened that the guy who was leading that knew of my performances in Trinidad because he had seen me perform…
